title: The Scientific Case Against Net Zero Falsifying the Greenhouse Gas Hypothesis

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4 (economic consequences paragraph)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states Net Zero is 'likely to cost each household in the UK £78,000 to decarbonise power generation and £58,000 to decarbonise road transport' and then says 'All this expenditure, ~£300,000 per household in total'. £78,000 + £58,000 = £136,000, not ~£300,000. No other per-household components are given to make up the difference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Sections 1 and 4 (cost estimates)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Three mutually incompatible cost magnitudes are given for the same policy: 'circa £3 trillion or more' (Section 1), a 'net cost of £321 billion' (Section 4), and '~£300,000 per household' which, for ~28 million UK households, implies ~£8.4 trillion. These cannot all be correct and no reconciliation is offered.

predicted_errors.error_location: Eq. (3)/(4) and associated numbers for Figure 1
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The IPCC forcing expression is F = 5.35·ln(C/C0) (natural logarithm), not 'Log'. Using ln, doubling 400→800 ppmv gives F = 3.71 W m⁻², so ΔT = 0.4×3.71 = 1.48 °C and 0.5×3.71 = 1.85 °C. The paper's quoted 0.64 °C and 0.81 °C are obtained only by using log base 10, i.e. the results are wrong by a factor of ~2.3, and the entire 'negligible warming' conclusion rests on this error.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section following Figure 1 ('The upper limit is ~0.81°C')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: A logarithmic forcing law is unbounded; it has no 'upper limit'. The value 0.81 °C is simply the value of the (mis-computed) formula at 800 ppmv, not a physical ceiling on possible warming. Describing it as 'an upper limit to the temperature change which can occur by adding greenhouse gases' is an unsupported extrapolation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Ideal Gas Law section, Eq. (2) T = PM/ρR and Table 1 discussion
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Deriving temperature from measured pressure and measured density is circular: the measured density of a planetary atmosphere is itself determined by its temperature (ρ = PM/RT). The 'excellent agreement' with observed temperatures is therefore guaranteed by construction and cannot test, let alone 'debunk', any radiative mechanism for Venus or Earth.

predicted_errors.error_location: Variable list after Eqs. (1)-(2)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'R = gas constant (m³ K⁻¹ mole⁻¹ kg) = 8.314' gives dimensionally incorrect units; R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ (= Pa m³ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹). Also P is stated in kPa and M as 'mean molecular weight' without units; with the stated units Eq. (2) is dimensionally inconsistent unless M is in g mol⁻¹ and P in kPa, which is not stated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Ideal Gas Law section ('The ideal gas law is robust and works for all gases')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: This contradicts both basic physical chemistry and the paper's own Table 1 note describing Venus's atmosphere as '96.5% supercritical carbon dioxide' — a regime in which the ideal gas law is explicitly invalid. The text also writes 'n = the number of moles of a real gas' while using the ideal gas equation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Ideal Gas Law section (33 K residual attributed to 'adiabatic auto-compression')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Static compression of an atmosphere cannot maintain a steady-state surface temperature above the radiative equilibrium temperature; a one-off compression produces no continuing energy source. The claim is asserted with no energy-balance derivation and would violate the first/second laws if a steady 33 K elevation were sustained without a radiative mechanism.

predicted_errors.error_location: Anthropogenic CO₂ calculation, Eq. labelled (1) (Ea% = 32.7/760 = 4.3%)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The fraction of an annual gross flux that is anthropogenic (4.3%) is then applied to the atmospheric stock ('with 420ppmv CO₂ in air the total accumulated anthropogenic part is (4.3%) ~18ppmv'). This is an invalid inference: natural gross fluxes are nearly balanced, so the anthropogenic share of a one-year flux says nothing about the accumulated anthropogenic increment. The text also undermines itself by noting the annual anthropogenic flux is 4.19 ppmv/yr, i.e. the claimed 'accumulated' 18 ppmv corresponds to only ~4 years of emissions.

predicted_errors.error_location: Human Breathing paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Two different values are given for the same quantity in consecutive sentences: 'With 7 billion people breathing would produce ~0.1638ppmv of CO₂ in air' and then '0.1268ppmv resting'. The subsequent projection (10.4 billion → ~0.24 ppmv) scales from 0.1638, confirming 0.1268 is erroneous.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph citing Skrable et al. (2022) and Berry (2020, 2021)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text reports 'accumulated human CO₂ is 11% of CO₂ in air or ~46.84 ppmv' and in the next sentence that Berry 'agrees with Harde (2017a) that human CO₂ adds about 18 ppmv'. These values differ by a factor of ~2.6 and are presented as mutually supporting without acknowledging the contradiction.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph on COVID and 1970s oil crisis / Keeling curve
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'two periods in recent times reduced human CO₂ emissions by as much as 20% (covid 2020–2023 and 1970s oil crisis)'. Global fossil CO₂ emissions fell by roughly 5–7% in 2020 only (rebounding in 2021), and the 1970s oil crises produced no ~20% global reduction. The premise of the argument is factually false.

predicted_errors.error_location: 'Burning Fossil Fuels' paragraph vs Harde calculation
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'Burning Fossil Fuels: 10,000million tonnes of CO₂ (i.e. 10Pg)' contradicts both reality (global fossil-fuel CO₂ emissions are ~35–37 Gt CO₂/yr) and the paper's own figure of Ea = 32.7 Pg/yr for total anthropogenic emissions given a few paragraphs earlier.

predicted_errors.error_location: 'Logistics' paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'Logistics: 8Gt CO₂ ... (~25% from man-made sources or ~1% of total CO₂ in air) ~1.03ppmv CO₂'. 1.03 ppmv out of 420 ppmv is 0.25% of CO₂ in air, not ~1%. The percentage quoted is a confusion between a share of annual emissions and a share of atmospheric burden.

predicted_errors.error_location: Residence-time discussion (Harde, 2017; IPCC; Equivalence Principle paragraph)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The IPCC does not claim different residence times for anthropogenic versus natural CO₂ molecules; it distinguishes molecular residence time (~4 years) from the adjustment/perturbation time of a CO₂ pulse (centuries). The paper misattributes a position to the IPCC and then 'refutes' it, and invokes a 'Principle of Equivalence' sourced to a dictionary definition of the word 'equivalence', not to any physical principle.

predicted_errors.error_location: Residence time values
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The residence time in the atmosphere was calculated to be approximately 3 to 5 years', later 'approximately 5 years', and later still 'between 3.0 and 4.1 years using the IPCC's own data'. These ranges are inconsistent with one another and attributed to the same sources.

predicted_errors.error_location: Weather-station siting paragraph (Watts, 2009; Watts, 2022; Fall et al., 2011)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Fall et al. (2011) is cited in support of 'artificial increases in measured temperatures in the USA'. That paper explicitly concluded that siting quality affected diurnal temperature range but had no significant effect on the mean temperature trend — the opposite of the claim it is cited for.

predicted_errors.error_location: Extreme-weather paragraph ('all in agreement with the IPCC views on the science')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim that there has been 'no increase in floods, droughts, hurricanes... no increase in extreme weather events' is attributed as being 'in agreement with' IPCC assessments (Field et al. 2012; Solomon et al. 2007; Stocker et al. 2013). IPCC reports in fact assess increases in several extreme classes (heat extremes, heavy precipitation) with high confidence; the attribution misrepresents the cited sources.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph on the Summaries for Policy Makers
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'It appears that the SPM is written by governments and activists before the scientific assessment is reached'. The SPM is drafted from, and approved line-by-line after, the underlying assessment chapters; the claim is contrary to documented IPCC procedure and is supported only by advocacy-press citations (Ball 2011, 2014, 2016).

predicted_errors.error_location: Keeling Curve paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'This curve does not correlate with global average surface temperature which has fluctuated in the same period'. Over 1958–2023 both the Mauna Loa CO₂ record and global mean surface temperature show strong monotonic increases; the correlation is in fact very high. No statistic is presented to support the assertion of non-correlation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Kinetic-theory/collision paragraph
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'the major components of air (nitrogen and oxygen) retain most of the energy ... and emit radiation at longer wavelengths'. N₂ and O₂ are homonuclear diatomics with no electric dipole moment and are essentially IR-inactive; they do not emit significant thermal infrared radiation. Collisional thermalisation is in fact the mechanism by which CO₂ emits at local temperature, not a reason it cannot affect radiative balance.

predicted_errors.error_location: Comment on the IPCC AR4 greenhouse definition ('radiation will be emitted at longer wavelengths...')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The claim that the atmosphere can restore energy balance by shifting emission to 'other areas of the electromagnetic spectrum where greenhouse gases do not absorb' without a temperature change contradicts Planck's law: the emitted spectrum is fixed by temperature and emissivity, so re-balancing at fixed temperature in this manner is impossible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Coe et al. discussion ('absorption is logarithmic (Beer-Lambert Law of attenuation)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Beer–Lambert law gives absorbance linear in concentration and transmittance exponential in concentration; it does not give a logarithmic dependence of forcing on concentration. The quasi-logarithmic CO₂ forcing arises from band-wing saturation across a spectrally structured absorption band, not from Beer–Lambert attenuation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction ('The climate operates with negative feedback (Le Chatelier's Principle)')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Le Chatelier's principle is a qualitative rule for shifts in chemical equilibria; it is not a theorem about feedbacks in open, forced, non-equilibrium geophysical systems and cannot be used to establish that climate feedbacks are net negative.

predicted_errors.error_location: Discussion of van Wijngaarden & Happer (2020, 2021)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: These papers compute a forcing of roughly 3 W m⁻² for doubled CO₂ and a corresponding no-feedback warming of order 1–1.4 K; they are here represented as finding 'only a very small increase in temperature' consistent with a ~0.5 °C sensitivity, which misstates their reported results.

predicted_errors.error_location: Coe et al. (2021) summary sentence
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'climate sensitivity to doubling concentration of CO₂ is (0.5°C) including 0.06°C from CH₄ and 0.08°C from N₂O' is internally incoherent: contributions from doubling CH₄ and N₂O cannot be part of the sensitivity to doubling CO₂. The cited values are for separate gases and have been conflated.

predicted_errors.error_location: Lindzen & Happer (2024) paragraph vs. claimed CO₂ sensitivity
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper claims total sensitivity to a CO₂ doubling is only ~0.5 °C, yet also states that achieving Net Zero 'will have a negligible effect on temperature ~0.28°C'. On the paper's own numbers, 0.28 °C is more than half of the entire doubling response and cannot consistently be described as negligible.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference list vs in-text citations (throughout)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Numerous works central to the argument are cited in the text but absent from the reference list, e.g. Coe et al. (2021) (the basis of the claimed 0.5 °C sensitivity), Seim and Olsen (2020), Allmendinger (2017), Alimonti et al. (2022) (quoted with a page number), Harde (2017a) and Harde (2014), Easterbrook (2016), Plimer (2009/2017/2021), Ball (2011/2014/2016), Statistics Norway (2023), Salby (2012/2013), Green & Britten (1998). Conversely, several listed references (e.g. Beck 2007, Meijer 2007, Boos & Storelvmo 2016, Nordt et al. 2003, Robinson et al. 2007, Rofe 2018, Kamis 2021) are never cited in the text.

predicted_errors.error_location: In-text 'Field, 2019' vs reference 'Field, T. (2013)'; 'Berry, 2019' vs references Berry (2020)/(2021)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The same quoted interview is cited as '(Field, 2019)' and '(Field, 2013)'; the reference list contains only Field (2013). Likewise 'contravenes the Equivalence Principle (Berry, 2019)' has no matching 2019 entry — only Berry (2020) and Berry (2021).

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference list: Mudge, F. B. (2012), Weather, 52(1), 13-17
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Weather volume 52 corresponds to 1997, not 2012; Mudge's paper on the Victorian-era development of greenhouse theory was published in Weather 52(1) in 1997. The year and volume are inconsistent.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference list: Washington et al. (2009), PNAS 109(49), 20564-20571, doi 10.1073/pnas.0711850106
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Volume 109 corresponds to 2012, whereas the stated year (2009) and the DOI suffix (…0711850106) correspond to volume 106. The volume number is wrong/internally inconsistent with the DOI and year.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference list: Archer et al. (2009) and Notz & Schellnhuber (2009)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Both references are given identical page ranges, 'PNAS 106(49), 20590-20595', for two different papers. Archer et al.'s methane-hydrate paper occupies a different page range (20596–20601); the duplication indicates a transcription error.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference list: Fyfe, Gillett & Zwiers (2013), Nature Climate Change, 3(9), 967-969
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The commentary 'Overestimated global warming over the past 20 years' appeared at Nature Climate Change 3, 767–769; the page numbers given are incorrect.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 1 (referred to in the Ideal Gas Law section)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text states 'The average near-surface temperature for planetary bodies ... is in excellent agreement with measured values (Table 1)', but no Table 1 is presented — only a 'Sources/Notes' block. The central quantitative claim of this section is therefore unverifiable from the paper.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 1 (Delta T vs CO₂ concentration)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The 'figure' is rendered as a degenerate table whose only content is a y-axis list (0–0.9) and an x-axis list (0–1000 ppmv), with no plotted data. Moreover, with the baseline implied by the text (C₀ = 400 ppmv) the λ = 0.5 curve would reach ~1.07 °C at 1000 ppmv, exceeding the stated 0.9 axis maximum, so the axes cannot be reconciled with the described calculation.

predicted_errors.error_location: Reference to 'the Keeling curve (figure 2)'
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The text refers to 'figure 2' but no figure with that number or caption exists; the only figures presented are an uncaptioned image and 'Figure 1. Delta T vs CO₂ concentration'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods section ('A literature review was carried out ... evidence-based approach')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No search strategy, databases, inclusion/exclusion criteria, or appraisal procedure are given; the stated evidence base consists largely of books, advocacy-organisation reports, blogs, YouTube talks and preprints selected for agreement with the authors' conclusion. This directly contradicts the paper's own criticism that IPCC literature is 'cherry picked' and its stated principle that 'Only empirical scientifically established facts should be considered'.

predicted_errors.error_location: Introduction (Frank, 2010; Statistics Norway, 2023)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: 'the increase in temperature from 1880 through 2000 is statistically indistinguishable from 0°K' misrepresents Frank (2010), which argued for a large lower-limit uncertainty envelope, not that the observed ~0.6–0.7 °C trend is zero. The sentence also contradicts the paper's own subsequent statement that observed warming is 'less than predicted by climate models', which presupposes a non-zero observed trend.

predicted_errors.error_location: Paragraph on thermal conductivity / back radiation ('the IPCC's attribution of 80% of warming to water vapor (~5% in air) and 20% to CO₂')
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: No IPCC report makes an 80%/20% attribution of warming between water vapour and CO₂ (water vapour is treated as a feedback, not a forcing), and the stated global water-vapour concentration of '~5% in air' is far above the global mean (~0.25% by volume). Both the attribution and the concentration figure are wrong.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3 (Climate Change Act description)
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Climate Change Act 2008 sets a target for net UK greenhouse gas emissions (CO₂-equivalent), not 'carbon dioxide (CO₂) emissions' specifically, and no 2022 amendment to the Act 'incentivized the transition away from fossil fuels with subsidies of so-called clean energy for businesses'; no legislative citation is given for this claimed amendment.

predicted_errors.error_location: Equation numbering (PV = nRT labelled (1); Ea% labelled (1))
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Two different equations are both numbered '(1)' (the ideal gas law and the anthropogenic percentage calculation), and the forcing/temperature equations are numbered (3) and (4) with no equation numbered consistently in between, making cross-referencing ambiguous.
